claims.claim: The study identified ~200 genes encoding extracellular proteins that exhibited ≥3-fold difference in microarray expression levels amongst the neuronal subtypes.
claims.source: We identified ~200 genes encoding extracellular proteins that exhibited ≥3-fold difference in microarray expression levels amongst the neuronal subtypes.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the microarray differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: 65 genes were selected as primary candidates based on domains and known players in cell-cell recognition.
claims.source: Based on the domains present in each protein and known players involved in cell-cell recognition, we selected 65 genes as primary candidates and cloned them from retinal cDNA (Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the candidate selection process.

claims.claim: The 65 primary candidate genes comprised 121 distinct cDNAs, including 15 splice variants that have not been previously reported.
claims.source: Because many of the genes encode more than one protein isoform as a result of alternative splicing or proteolytic cleavage, these primary candidates comprised 121 distinct cDNAs, including 15 splice variants that have not been previously reported (Figure 1—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cloning and characterization of candidate genes.

claims.claim: New splice variants were identified for Ncam1, Netrin5, several Semaphorins and all four Unc5s.
claims.source: New splice variants were identified for Ncam1, Netrin5, several Semaphorins and all four Unc5s (i.e. Unc5A-D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cloning and characterization of candidate genes.

claims.claim: The candidate proteins fall into three categories: secreted (26/121; 22%), GPI-linked (17/121; 14%) and type I transmembrane (78/121; 64%).
claims.source: The candidate proteins fall into three categories: secreted (26/121; 22%), GPI-linked (17/121; 14%) and type I transmembrane (78/121; 64%).
claims.evidence: This is a categorization of the candidate proteins based on their structural features.

claims.claim: For AP-tagged proteins, 106 out of 121 (88%) proteins were produced at optimal concentrations.
claims.source: For AP-tagged proteins, 106 out of 121 (88%) proteins were produced at optimal concentrations; for Fc-tagged proteins, 110 out of 121 (91%) proteins were produced at optimal concentrations (see Materials and methods) (Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the recombinant protein production, with supporting Western blot data in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: For Fc-tagged proteins, 110 out of 121 (91%) proteins were produced at optimal concentrations.
claims.source: For AP-tagged proteins, 106 out of 121 (88%) proteins were produced at optimal concentrations; for Fc-tagged proteins, 110 out of 121 (91%) proteins were produced at optimal concentrations (see Materials and methods) (Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the recombinant protein production, with supporting Western blot data in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Interactions at the cell surface exhibit low affinities (KD ~ µM) and fast dissociation rates.
claims.source: It is largely the case that interactions at the cell surface exhibit low affinities (KD ~ µM) and fast dissociation rates (Vandermerwe and Barclay, 1994), kinetic properties that allow transient, contact-dependent interactions to occur between recognition proteins expressed on neighboring cells in vivo but often make biochemical detection in vitro difficult.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about cell surface protein interactions, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The ELISA-based binding assay tetramerizes the AP-tagged receptor and Fc-tagged ligand proteins.
claims.source: Our ELISA-based binding assay surmounts this limitation because it utilizes a strategy that tetramerizes the AP-tagged receptor and Fc-tagged ligand proteins (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the assay methodology.

claims.claim: By inducing tetramers, the assay is highly sensitive allowing proteins with micromolar affinities to be detected at nanomolar concentrations.
claims.source: By inducing tetramers, which provides additive or avidity effects, the assay is highly sensitive allowing proteins with micromolar affinities to be detected at nanomolar concentrations.
claims.evidence: This explains the sensitivity advantage of the tetramerization strategy.

claims.claim: The study tested 126 proteins for binding in a matrix which reciprocally tests every pair-wise combination (126 x 126 = 15,876 binding reactions).
claims.source: We tested the 126 proteins for binding in a matrix which reciprocally tests every pair-wise combination (i.e. 126 x 126 = 15,876 binding reactions) (Figure 2; Visser et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the scale of the binding screen, with results shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The screen includes 126 homophilic pairs and 7,875 unique heterophilic pairs.
claims.source: This includes 126 homophilic pairs and 7,875 unique heterophilic pairs.
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on the matrix design.

claims.claim: Interacting proteins were defined as those that exhibited ≥5-fold binding above background levels.
claims.source: Interacting proteins identified in the screen were defined as those that exhibited ≥5-fold binding above background levels.
claims.evidence: This describes the threshold used to identify positive interactions.

claims.claim: The study identified 192 unique interaction pairs.
claims.source: Using this criteria, we identified 192 unique interaction pairs, ~50 of which, to our knowledge, have not been reported in the literature (Figure 3 and Figure 4; Visser et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a primary result from the binding screen.

claims.claim: Of 109 expected positive control interaction pairs, 91 were identified, giving a false negative rate of 17%.
claims.source: Of these 109 positive control interaction pairs, we identified 91 giving us a false negative rate of 17%.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the screen's sensitivity based on known interactions.

claims.claim: The false negative rate of 17% is lower than published values for yeast-two-hybrid screens which give rise to false negative rates between 28 and 51%.
claims.source: This frequency is lower than published values for the yeast-two-hybrid screen which gives rise to false negative rates between 28 and 51% (Huang and Bader, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to another screening method, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: All three FLRT (FLRT1-3) and all four Unc5 (Unc5A-D) family members exhibited interactions in the screen.
claims.source: Interactions between all three FLRT (FLRT1-3) and all four Unc5 (Unc5A-D) family members were observed in the screen; and all pairs exhibited high levels of binding at or near the level of saturation of detection (mean Abs650nm value = 2.14).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the binding screen.

claims.claim: All FLRT-Unc5 pairs exhibited high levels of binding at or near the level of saturation of detection (mean Abs650nm value = 2.14).
claims.source: Interactions between all three FLRT (FLRT1-3) and all four Unc5 (Unc5A-D) family members were observed in the screen; and all pairs exhibited high levels of binding at or near the level of saturation of detection (mean Abs650nm value = 2.14).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the binding screen.

claims.claim: Prior to the screen, four FLRT-Unc5 interactions had been described in the literature (three in mouse and one in zebrafish).
claims.source: Furthermore, of the 12 possible FLRT-Unc5 interactions (i.e. 3 FLRTs x 4 Unc5s), prior to our screen, four had been described in the literature (three in mouse and one in zebrafish) (Karaulanov et al., 2009; Sollner and Wright, 2009; Yamagishi et al., 2011) suggesting that the eight new FLRT-Unc5 binding pairs we identified were likely to represent biologically-relevant interactions rather than false positives.
claims.evidence: This is a literature review statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: The study identified eight new FLRT-Unc5 binding pairs.
claims.source: Furthermore, of the 12 possible FLRT-Unc5 interactions (i.e. 3 FLRTs x 4 Unc5s), prior to our screen, four had been described in the literature (three in mouse and one in zebrafish) (Karaulanov et al., 2009; Sollner and Wright, 2009; Yamagishi et al., 2011) suggesting that the eight new FLRT-Unc5 binding pairs we identified were likely to represent biologically-relevant interactions rather than false positives.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the binding screen, inferred from the total possible interactions minus previously known ones.

claims.claim: Concentration-dependent binding curves were observed for all FLRT-Unc5 interactions tested in titration experiments.
claims.source: In all cases, we observed concentration-dependent binding curves.
claims.evidence: This is a result from titration binding experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The FLRT-Unc5 binding constants observed in titration curves (on the order of ~1–10 nM) are much higher than published affinities using monomeric protein in surface plasmon resonance experiments (0.3-21 μM).
claims.source: Because the extracellular region of the proteins used in these titration curves is tetramerized, the FLRT-Unc5 binding constants we observed (i.e. on the order of ~1–10 nM) are much higher than published affinities using monomeric protein in surface plasmon resonance experiments (0.3-21 μM) (Seiradake et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of binding affinities between different assay formats, with a citation to published data.

claims.claim: All combinations of FLRTs and Unc5s interact between opposing cells as evidenced by cell aggregation.
claims.source: Using the cell aggregation assay, we tested every combination of FLRTs and Unc5s and found that all pairs interact between opposing cells as evidenced by cell aggregation (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from cell aggregation assays shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: No clusters were observed between mock transfected cells, FLRT-FLRT or Unc5-Unc5 expressing cells.
claims.source: By contrast, no clusters were observed between mock transfected cells, FLRT-FLRT or Unc5-Unc5 expressing cells.
claims.evidence: This is a negative control result from cell aggregation assays.

claims.claim: Trans interactions occur between all FLRT-Unc5 pairs.
claims.source: Together these data confirm that, as observed in our binding screen, trans interactions occur between all FLRT-Unc5 pairs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell aggregation assay results.

claims.claim: The majority of neurons did not respond to FLRT or Unc5 stripes, growing indiscriminately across them.
claims.source: While the majority of neurons did not respond to FLRT or Unc5 stripes, growing indiscriminately across them, we observed small populations of neurons (5-18%) that responded to FLRT1 (n=61/375, 16% attractive; n=19/375, 5% repulsive), FLRT2 (n=63/344; 18% repulsive), FLRT3 (n=37/438, 8% attractive; n=33/438, 8% repulsive), Unc5C (n=45/396, 11% repulsive) and Unc5D (n=49/407, 12% repulsive) stripes (Figure 5A-I).

claims.claim: Unc5C, Unc5D, and all three FLRTs mediate recognition events between subtypes of retinal neurons.
claims.source: Together these data demonstrate that Unc5C, Unc5D, and all three FLRTs mediate recognition events between subtypes of retinal neurons and suggest that FLRTs and Unc5s may contribute to development of the retinal circuit.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stripe assay results.

claims.claim: FLRTs and Unc5s may contribute to development of the retinal circuit.
claims.source: Together these data demonstrate that Unc5C, Unc5D, and all three FLRTs mediate recognition events between subtypes of retinal neurons and suggest that FLRTs and Unc5s may contribute to development of the retinal circuit.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the functional data.

claims.claim: All FLRT and Unc5 antibodies were highly specific with little to no cross-reactivity as assessed by ELISA using purified protein.
claims.source: All FLRT and Unc5 antibodies were highly specific with little to no cross-reactivity as assessed by ELISA using purified protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: At P6, FLRT1 expression was largely restricted to neurites that arborize in S1.
claims.source: At P6 we observed laminar-restricted expression patterns for all FLRTs and three out of the four Unc5s (Figure 6). FLRT1 expression was largely restricted to neurites that arborize in S1 (Figure 6A)

claims.evidence: This is a result from immunostaining shown in Figure 6B.

claims.evidence: This is a result from immunostaining shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: At P6, Unc5A was highly expressed in the cell body layers flanking the IPL and, within the IPL, was expressed in neurites that arborize in S1/2/3/5.
claims.source: Unc5A was highly expressed in the cell body layers flanking the IPL and, within the IPL, was expressed in neurites that arborize in S1/2/3/5 (Figure 6D)

claims.claim: At P6, Unc5D expression was largely restricted to S1/5.
claims.source: Unc5D expression was largely restricted to S1/5.

claims.claim: At P6, Unc5B did not show laminar restriction—it was expressed at low levels uniformly across the IPL.
claims.source: Unc5B did not show laminar restriction—it was expressed at low levels uniformly across the IPL (Figure 6E).

claims.claim: Laminar-restricted expression of FLRT1-3 and Unc5A,C,D is spatio-temporally regulated.
claims.source: Comparison of the expression patterns observed at P6 with the patterns observed at P2 and P4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) demonstrates that laminar-restricted expression of FLRT1-3 and Unc5A,C,D is spatio-temporally regulated.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing expression patterns across developmental time points shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: FLRT2 and Unc5C showed broad expression across the IPL at P2 that gradually became sublamina-restricted by P6.
claims.source: One subset of proteins, FLRT2 and Unc5C, showed broad expression across the IPL at P2 that gradually became sublamina-restricted by P6.
claims.evidence: This is a description of developmental expression patterns observed across time points.

claims.claim: FLRT1 and FLRT3 showed sublaminar bias already at P2 that changed only slightly as the IPL expanded with age.
claims.source: A second group, FLRT1 and FLRT3, showed sublaminar bias already at P2 that changed only slightly as the IPL expanded with age.
claims.evidence: This is a description of developmental expression patterns observed across time points.

claims.claim: Unc5A and Unc5D added new sublayers at later ages.
claims.source: The final group, Unc5A and Unc5D, added new sublayers at later ages: Unc5A was not observed in the IPL until P6, even though immunoreactivity was detected in neuronal somata at earlier ages, suggesting that IPL innervation by Unc5A-positive cells happens later than other family members.
claims.evidence: This is a description of developmental expression patterns observed across time points.

claims.claim: Unc5A was not observed in the IPL until P6, even though immunoreactivity was detected in neuronal somata at earlier ages.
claims.source: Unc5A was not observed in the IPL until P6, even though immunoreactivity was detected in neuronal somata at earlier ages, suggesting that IPL innervation by Unc5A-positive cells happens later than other family members.
claims.evidence: This is a result from immunostaining across developmental time points.

claims.claim: IPL innervation by Unc5A-positive cells happens later than other family members.
claims.source: Unc5A was not observed in the IPL until P6, even though immunoreactivity was detected in neuronal somata at earlier ages, suggesting that IPL innervation by Unc5A-positive cells happens later than other family members.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the temporal expression pattern of Unc5A.

claims.claim: Unc5D exhibited S1 restriction at P2-4 and then added expression in S5 at P6.
claims.source: Unc5D, meanwhile, exhibited S1 restriction at P2-4 and then added expression in S5 at P6.
claims.evidence: This is a description of developmental expression patterns observed across time points.

claims.claim: The expression pattern of Unc5D may remain dynamic after P6, as S5 expression is maintained while S1 expression is lost by P8.
claims.source: Interestingly, the expression pattern of Unc5D may remain dynamic after P6, as immunostaining published by Feldheim and colleagues suggests that, while S5 expression is maintained, S1 expression is lost by P8 (Sweeney et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on published data from another study.

claims.claim: Between P2 and P4, Unc5C and FLRT2 expression patterns become restricted to complementary sublaminae in the IPL with Unc5C concentrated in S1/3/5 and FLRT2 predominantly expressed in S2/4.

claims.evidence: This is a result from immunostaining across developmental time points shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Complementary expression of FLRT2 and Unc5C suggests that these lamina-specific stratifications may arise due to repulsive interactions between neuronal subtypes expressing FLRT2 and Unc5C.
claims.source: Complementary expression suggests that these lamina-specific stratifications may arise due to repulsive interactions between neuronal subtypes expressing FLRT2 and Unc5C.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the expression pattern data.

claims.claim: Repulsive signaling of Unc5 in response to ligand binding has been well-established.
claims.source: Repulsive signaling of Unc5 in response to ligand binding has been well-established (for review of Netrin1-induced repulsion see Moore et al., 2007; for FLRT2-induced repulsion via Unc5D see Yamagishi et al., 2011).

claims.claim: FLRT2 is sufficient to mediate repulsion in response to Unc5C.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain-of-function stripe assay results.

claims.claim: Repulsive signaling can occur downstream of FLRT2.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that FLRT2 is sufficient to mediate repulsion in response to Unc5C and, as such, repulsive signaling can occur downstream of FLRT2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain-of-function stripe assay results.

claims.claim: Flrt2 is expressed by a subset of cells that includes SACs, a sparse non-SAC population in the inner nuclear layer, and a non-SAC population in the ganglion cell layer.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that Flrt2 is expressed by a subset of cells that includes: 1) SACs; 2) a sparse non-SAC population in the inner nuclear layer (INL) (presumably amacrines due to their laminar position close to the IPL and the fact that bipolar cells are not yet born at P1); and 3) a non-SAC population in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) that, based upon their large soma size, are likely to be retinal ganglion cells (Figure 7A).

results.result: The authors used microarray data from 13 neuronal subtypes and bioinformatics approaches to identify ~200 differentially-expressed extracellular proteins, from which 65 genes (121 distinct cDNAs including 15 novel splice variants) were selected as primary candidates for the binding screen.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C28 describe a systematic bioinformatics pipeline starting from microarray data (C2, C20-C21), applying prediction algorithms (C22-C23), identifying differentially-expressed genes (C24), and selecting candidates (C25-C28). The methodology is clearly described with specific numbers and tools cited, and the identification of novel splice variants (C26-C27) represents a concrete discovery. The workflow is documented in supplementary figures.

results.result: The authors successfully produced recombinant AP-tagged (106/121, 88%) and Fc-tagged (110/121, 91%) proteins at optimal concentrations for the binding screen.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 report high success rates for protein production with specific quantitative data and reference to Western blot validation in supplementary figures. This technical achievement is well-documented and essential for the subsequent binding screen.

results.result: The authors developed and validated a high-throughput ELISA-based binding assay that tetramerizes proteins to detect low-affinity interactions, screening 126×126 protein pairs (15,876 reactions) and identifying 192 unique interaction pairs with a 17% false negative rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C39 describe the assay methodology (C31-C33), scale (C34-C35), threshold criteria (C36), and validation (C37-C39). The false negative rate of 17% is calculated from known positive controls (91/109 detected) and compares favorably to yeast-two-hybrid screens (C39). The tetramerization strategy is well-justified for detecting weak interactions, and the comprehensive matrix design is clearly documented.

results.result: The binding screen identified ~50 previously-unknown receptor-ligand pairs, including 8 new FLRT-Unc5 interactions (in addition to 4 previously known), with all 12 FLRT-Unc5 pairs showing high binding levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C40-C43 report the discovery of novel interactions with specific focus on FLRT-Unc5 families. The quantification is clear (8 new + 4 known = 12 total possible pairs), and the high binding signal (mean Abs650nm = 2.14, C41) provides strong biochemical evidence. The prior literature is appropriately cited (C42).

results.result: Titration binding experiments and cell aggregation assays confirmed that all FLRT-Unc5 pairs interact in trans with concentration-dependent binding, while no homophilic FLRT-FLRT or Unc5-Unc5 interactions were observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 provide orthogonal validation of the screen results using two independent assays. The titration curves show concentration-dependence (C44), the comparison to published SPR data is appropriate (C45), and the cell aggregation assay demonstrates trans interactions (C46-C48). The negative controls (C47) strengthen the specificity of the findings.

results.result: The screen identified 24 previously-unreported Semaphorin-Neuropilin or Semaphorin-Plexin interactions and confirmed 4 genetically-suggested interactions, revealing that Nrp1/2 can directly bind Sema4/6 families and some Sema3s can bind Plexins without Neuropilins.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 report novel findings about Semaphorin family interactions that challenge existing models. The comprehensive testing of all family members (20 Sema, 9 Plxn, 2 Nrp) provides systematic evidence, and the discovery of direct Sema3-Plexin interactions (C112) is particularly significant as it expands beyond the known Sema3E-PlxnD1 interaction.

results.result: Stripe assays revealed that small subpopulations (5-18%) of retinal neurons respond to FLRT1, FLRT2, FLRT3, Unc5C, and Unc5D with attraction or repulsion, while the majority of neurons grow permissively and Unc5A/B show minimal or no specific responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C60 provide detailed quantitative data from stripe assays with specific cell counts for each protein tested. The observation that only subpopulations respond (C49-C50) is consistent with subtype-specific recognition, and the negative results for Unc5A/B (C58-C60) serve as important controls. The single-cell resolution methodology is appropriate for the heterogeneous retinal neuron population.

results.result: The authors conclude that Unc5C, Unc5D, and all three FLRTs mediate recognition events between retinal neuron subtypes and may contribute to retinal circuit development.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 represent reasonable conclusions from the stripe assay data (C49-C60). C61 is a direct interpretation of the functional data, while C62 is appropriately qualified as speculative ('may contribute'). The functional responses observed are consistent with a role in circuit development, though definitive proof would require genetic loss-of-function studies.

results.result: At P6, FLRT1-3 and Unc5A,C,D exhibit distinct laminar-restricted expression patterns in the IPL (FLRT1 in S1, FLRT2 in S2/4, FLRT3 in S3, Unc5A in S1/2/3/5, Unc5C in S1/3/5, Unc5D in S1/5), while Unc5B shows uniform expression, as validated by highly specific antibodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70 describe laminar expression patterns with specific sublayer assignments based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 6. The antibody specificity is validated by ELISA (C63), and the complementary expression of FLRT2 (S2/4) and Unc5C (S1/3/5) is particularly notable. The patterns are clearly documented with both images and quantitative fluorescence profiles.

results.result: Developmental analysis (P2-P6) reveals that FLRT and Unc5 expression is spatio-temporally regulated with three patterns: initially diffuse becoming restricted (FLRT2, Unc5C), initially precise (FLRT1, FLRT3), and stepwise addition of sublayers (Unc5A, Unc5D).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 describe temporal dynamics of expression patterns across three developmental time points. The categorization into three developmental strategies is well-supported by the immunostaining data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2. The inference about Unc5A innervation timing (C76) is reasonable based on the observation of somatic but not IPL expression at early ages (C75). C78 appropriately cites published data for the P8 time point.

results.result: FLRT2 and Unc5C show complementary expression patterns (FLRT2 in S2/4, Unc5C in S1/3/5) that develop between P2-P4, and both proteins induce neurite attraction/repulsion in culture, positioning them to mediate laminar targeting through repulsive interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 and C79-C80 integrate expression data (C9, C79) with functional data (C7) to support a model of repulsive laminar targeting (C8, C80). The complementary expression pattern is a strong predictor of repulsive function, and the stripe assay data confirm that both proteins can elicit repulsion. However, C8 and C80 are appropriately qualified as inferences ('ideal position', 'may arise') rather than definitive proof.

results.result: Neurons repelled by Unc5C stripes express FLRT2 (26/26) and neurons repelled by FLRT2 stripes express Unc5C (30/30), supporting a model of bidirectional repulsive signaling between FLRT2- and Unc5C-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 provide strong correlative evidence linking receptor expression to functional response. The 100% correlation in both directions (C81, C83) is striking, and the negative results for FLRT1/3 (C82) demonstrate specificity. However, C84 represents a model rather than direct proof of bidirectional signaling, as the experiments show correlation but not mechanism. The model is reasonable but would require additional experiments to definitively establish bidirectional signaling.

results.result: Gain-of-function experiments demonstrate that ectopic FLRT2 expression is sufficient to confer repulsion by Unc5C stripes (39/39 neurons repelled), while Unc5C expression does not confer self-repulsion (27/28 permissive), indicating that repulsive signaling can occur downstream of FLRT2.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C87-C90 describe a well-controlled gain-of-function experiment. The 100% response rate in FLRT2-transfected neurons (C87) versus 96% permissive in Unc5C-transfected controls (C88) provides strong evidence for FLRT2 sufficiency (C89-C90). The caveat that other proteins might be recruited in cis is appropriately acknowledged in the text. This is a key experiment demonstrating that FLRTs can mediate repulsive signaling, which was not previously established.

results.result: Flrt2 is expressed by SACs (with temporal shift from ON SACs at P1 to OFF SACs at P6), a subset of ooDSGCs (~50% of CART+ cells), and other amacrine/RGC populations, while SACs do not express any Unc5 family members.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C100 provide detailed cell-type identification using multiple markers (calbindin for SACs, CART for ooDSGCs) and techniques (in situ hybridization, immunostaining of transgenic mice). The quantification of CART+/Flrt2+ cells (C94) and complete absence of Unc5 expression in SACs (C99-C100) are clearly documented. The temporal shift in SAC expression (C92-C93) is an interesting observation though its functional significance is unclear.

results.result: SACs are robustly repelled by Unc5C stripes (92%, 49/53) but not FLRT2 stripes (0%, 0/71), and since SACs express FLRT2 but not FLRT1/3, SAC repulsion by Unc5C likely involves FLRT2-Unc5C interactions that may contribute to SAC laminar organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 integrate expression data (C96-C98) with functional data (C101-C102) to support a specific model for SAC lamination (C103-C104). The high repulsion rate by Unc5C (C101) combined with FLRT2 expression and lack of FLRT1/3 expression provides strong correlative evidence. However, C103-C104 are appropriately qualified as inferences ('could be', 'may contribute') since definitive proof would require genetic manipulation.

results.result: Drd4-GFP ooDSGCs express FLRT2 and are repelled by Unc5C (7/7, 100%) but not FLRT2 (0/10, 0%), suggesting that at least one DSGC subtype may use FLRT2-Unc5C repulsive interactions for laminar restriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 extend the SAC findings to a postsynaptic partner population. Despite the small sample size (7 neurons for Unc5C, 10 for FLRT2), the 100% response rate and 0% response rate provide strong evidence. The conclusion (C107) is appropriately qualified ('may utilize') given that this is one DSGC subtype and genetic validation is lacking. The parallel use of the same molecular mechanism by synaptic partners is a significant finding.

results.result: The authors propose that evolution may have co-opted the same FLRT2-Unc5C repulsive mechanism in both SACs and ooDSGCs to ensure joint laminar restriction in S2/4, facilitating appropriate synaptic partner interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C135-C136 present an evolutionary model for coordinated lamination of synaptic partners. While the data show that both SACs and Drd4-GFP ooDSGCs express FLRT2 and are repelled by Unc5C, the model of 'co-option' is highly speculative (C14, C136). The proposal that this ensures 'joint laminar restriction' (C135) is reasonable but not directly tested—it remains possible that each cell type uses this mechanism independently. The model is intellectually appealing but lacks direct experimental support.

results.result: Different FLRT-Unc5 pairs exhibit differences in binding affinity, which may contribute to recognition specificity despite promiscuous binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 address an important question about specificity given promiscuous binding. C114 is supported by the titration curves in Figure 2C showing different binding profiles, though the authors note that saturation prevents precise KD determination. C115 is appropriately qualified as speculation. The analogy to cadherins is apt, though direct evidence that affinity differences mediate specificity in this system is lacking.

results.result: Published studies indicate FLRT homophilic binding is weak and difficult to detect, with structural evidence suggesting cis-dimerization, and the in vivo phenotype of FLRT mutations may reflect disrupted FLRT-latrophilin rather than FLRT-FLRT interactions; latrophilins are expressed in retina.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C125 accurately summarize published literature from other groups (Seiradake et al., Lu et al.) regarding FLRT homophilic interactions and FLRT-latrophilin binding. The authors appropriately cite these studies and note that their own screen did not detect FLRT homophilic interactions. C125 provides relevant context that latrophilins are expressed in retina, which could explain the attraction to FLRT1/3 observed in stripe assays. This is appropriate citation and contextualization of prior work.

results.result: Published studies show that Unc5D and Unc5B mediate repulsion in response to FLRT ligands in cortex and thalamus; the current study extends this to Unc5C in retina, suggesting repulsive signaling is a conserved function of Unc5 receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 appropriately cite prior work (C126-C127) and integrate it with the current findings (C129) to propose a general principle about Unc5 function (C128-C129). The inference that repulsive signaling is conserved across Unc5B, Unc5C, and Unc5D is reasonable given the data, though Unc5A remains untested in this context.

results.result: Bidirectional signaling is well-established for Eph-ephrin interactions, and a similar FLRT2-Unc5C bidirectional repulsion mechanism would provide an efficient solution for organizing FLRT2+ and Unc5C+ neurons into adjacent IPL layers.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 correctly cites established knowledge about Eph-ephrin bidirectional signaling. However, C131 is speculative—while the data show that both FLRT2+ and Unc5C+ neurons are repelled by their cognate ligands, direct evidence for bidirectional signaling (i.e., that a single FLRT2-Unc5C interaction triggers signaling in both cells simultaneously) is lacking. The model is plausible and the analogy to Eph-ephrin is appropriate, but experimental proof is needed.

results.result: Published genetic studies show that PlxnA2-Sema6A interactions influence SAC laminar choices, but most SAC dendrites still target correctly in mutants, suggesting additional parallel mechanisms exist for SAC laminar restriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 accurately summarize published genetic data from Sun et al. 2013 and draw a reasonable inference (C134) that additional mechanisms must exist. This provides important context for why identifying FLRT2-Unc5C as a candidate mechanism is significant—it could represent one of these parallel pathways. The logic is sound and the citation is appropriate.

results.result: The mouse retina IPL contains ~70 neuronal subtypes organized into five sublayers (S1-S5) where neurons synapse selectively on specific partners, requiring high specificity during circuit wiring.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C15-C19 provide established background knowledge about IPL organization, appropriately cited to review articles (C16-C17). This contextualizes why the IPL is a good model system for studying lamination and molecular recognition. The claims are factually accurate and well-supported by the literature.

results.result: The microarray analyses used P6 neurons, a developmental stage when extensive neurite extension, arbor refinement, laminar organization and synapse formation occur in the IPL.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 justifies the choice of P6 for microarray analysis based on developmental timing. This is appropriate experimental design as it targets a stage when the relevant developmental processes are active. The claim is supported by established knowledge of IPL development.
